case_name: Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital c. N.G.
text:
Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish
General Hospital c. N.G.

2019 QCCS 5420

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-109374-192

DATE:

September 17, 2019

_____________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

SUZANNE COURCHESNE, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

sir
mortimer b. davis jewish general hospital
administrated
by the
CIUSSS DU CENTRE-OUEst-de-l’île-de-montréal

and

dr.
louise miner

Plaintiffs

v.

N.
G.

Defendant

and

S.
G.

Interested person

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(
safeguard order
)

_____________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Plaintiffs (
collectively,
the Hospital
) seek the issuance of a safeguard order relating to Mr. N. G.

[
2
]

Mr. N. G. is a 78 year old man who has been
diagnosed with schizophrenia and narcissistic personality disorder.

[
3
]

He is currently confined in the Hospital’s
institution for a 30 day period pursuant to a judgment rendered by the Court of
Quebec on August 19, 2019.

[
4
]

On September 3, 2019, Mr. N. G. was served with the Hospital’s application to
obtain a court order for treatment (
the Application
). The Application
asks for the Hospital to be authorized to administer a treatment plan to Mr. N.
G., which includes the administration of antipsychotic medication in oral or
injectable form for a three year period as well as his hospitalization until a
safe discharge plan is in place.

[
5
]

On September 9, 2019, Mr. N. G., through his attorney, requested a postponement
of the hearing on the Application to allow him to retain an expert and contest
the demand. The hearing was postponed to September 16, 2019. On this date,
before the Court, Mr. N. G. reiterated his request and asked for a 3 month
delay in order to obtain a counter-expertise and to present his arguments in
contestation of the Application. The Hospital agreed to the postponement but
asked this Court to issue certain safeguard orders in the interim.

1.

THE APPLICABLE PRINCIPLES OF LAW

[
6
]

This request for a safeguard order must be analyzed under the following principles.

[
7
]

Every person is inviolable and is entitled to the integrity of his person. No
person may be made to undergo care of any nature without his consent, except
with the authorization of the court in the circumstances stated at
Article 16

of the
Civil Code of Quebec
(
C.C.Q
.) and within the
guidelines of
Article 12

C.C.Q.

[
8
]

The Court of Appeal in
F.D.
c.
Centre
universitaire de santé McGill, (Hôpital Royal-Victoria)
[1]
has mandated a
rigorous seven step analysis which must be followed by any court adjudicating
an application to obtain the authorization for care to a person of full age who
is incapable of consenting to treatment.

[
9
]

For the Court to issue a safeguard order, the
following requirements must be met:

1.

Urgency;

The demand must raise a serious
question to be tried;

Serious or irreparable harm must
result if the relief is not granted;

The balance of inconvenience must
weigh in favour of the party who is seeking the safeguard order.

2.

ANALYSIS AND DECISION

[
10
]

On the basis of the evidence presented at the hearing, although the Court does not have the
benefit of all relevant evidence that Mr. N. G. would like to present,
including a possible expert report and testimony, the Court considers that
safeguard measures must be issued for a period of three (3) months. This delay
will enable Mr. N. G. to retain an expert of his choice, be examined by
this expert and, should he maintain his opposition to the treatment plan, file
his expert report and contest the Application on December 16, 2019.

[
11
]

The hearing on the safeguard order lasted more than three hours during which
psychiatrist Dr. Carmella Roy and Mr. N. G. testified. Although Mr. N. G. was
represented by attorney, he personally intervened on numerous occasions, raised
several objections to questions and statements made by the opposing party and
was extremely insistent during the hearing.

[
12
]

The evidence presented before this Court includes the following exhibits:

•

The report of Dr.
Carmella Roy, dated August 26, 2019 (exhibit P-1);

•

The most recent court
order for treatment issued on April 4, 2016 for a duration of 3 years (exhibit
P-2);

•

The court order for temporary confinement to
undergo a psychiatric examination issued on August 15, 2019 and the medical
report in support thereof dated August 13, 2019 (exhibit P-3);

•

The court order for confinement in an
institution for a duration of 30 days, pursuant to a judgment rendered on
August 19, 2019 and the psychiatric examination reports filed in support, dated
August 15 and 16, 2019 (exhibit P-4).

[
13
]

Dr Carmella Roy, a geriatric psychiatrist who has been treating Mr. N. G.
during the current and past admissions at the Hospital’s institution, explained
that Mr. N. G. has been followed by their psychiatric services since 1999.
He has been admitted ten times, usually in a psychotic decompensation, often as
a result of medication non-compliance. Four previous court orders for treatment
were issued against him during the past 12 years. He has been non-compliant
with his prescribed medication since November 2018.

[
14
]

The event that triggered the most recent demands (for psychiatric
examination, for confinement and for treatment) concerns a harassing and
stalking behaviour that Mr. N. G. allegedly had towards his orthopedic
surgeon’s secretary.

2.1.

Urgency

[
15
]

According to the evidence, Mr. N. G. suffers
from schizophrenia and has ceased his medication since November 2018. Dr. Roy,
his treating psychiatrist during the current and past admissions, explained
that Mr. N. G.’s mental state has recently deteriorated, that he suffers from
psychotic decompensation and that he has become more paranoid, demanding,
insistent and intimidating.

[
16
]

Although at this point, Mr. N. G. has not been
physically aggressive or menacing, his behavior and inappropriate social
interactions are the result of his psychosis and constitute imminent risk of
deterioration if he remains untreated.

[
17
]

Furthermore, the order for confinement expires
imminently and Mr. N. G. is currently being kept in the High Care area of the
Hospital’s psychiatric ward. Hospitalization through an order of this Court
would provide Mr. N. G.’s treating team with greater flexibility to determine
the most appropriate environment for his treatment and, depending on his
clinical evolution, to progressively grant him certain privileges, as mentioned
by Dr. Roy at the hearing.

2.2.

Serious issue to be tried

[
18
]

In light of the evidence, despite Mr. N. G.’s
vehement contestation, the Court considers that there is a serious issue to be
tried, on the basis of the criteria developed by the
Court of Appeal in
Institut Philippe Pinel de Montréal c. A.G
.
[2]

and
F.D. c. Centre universitaire de santé McGill
(Hôpital Royal-Victoria)
[3]
;

[
19
]

The Hospital presents a strong case that Mr. N. G. is incapable of giving
consent, as demonstrated by the evidence and by his own testimony:

•

Although he understands the concept of
schizophrenia, Mr. N. G. denies his diagnosis; he does not believe that he is
mentally ill;

•

He understands the nature and the objectives of
the treatment but he does not acknowledge the benefits that this treatment could
have on his own health nor does he comprehend the risks for him of not
undergoing the recommended treatment;

•

His incapacity to understand his diagnosis and
the consequences of refusing the treatment are the result of his illness.

[
20
]

Mr. N. G. has categorically refused to take any antipsychotic medication
since November 2018.

[
21
]

The evidence also satisfies the Court that the
administration of oral or injectable antipsychotic medication, the
administration of any required adjunctive medications to manage possible
side-effects and the medical investigations to monitor Mr. N. G.’s clinical
evolution, as described by Dr. Roy, for a period of 3 months, are required and
in Mr. N. G.’s best interest, taking into account their purpose, anticipated
beneficial effects and risks associated therewith.

[
22
]

In light of Dr. Roy’s testimony and report, the
likely benefits of the treatment plan outweigh any possible negative effects.
The treating team will exercise close follow-up of Mr. N. G.’s health condition
and discuss with him, if he accepts to communicate, to determine the most
appropriate medication and dosage.

[
23
]

Mr. N. G. is undoubtedly a very intelligent and well-spoken person, with the
capacity to be a functional and useful individual within the community. When he
is under pharmacological treatment, Mr. N. G. is well and able to volunteer, an
activity that he particularly enjoys. Presently, he is not functional, he is
distressed and engages in inappropriate and intimidating behaviour, as
demonstrated by the psychiatric reports and the testimony of his treating
psychiatrist.

2.3.

Serious or irreparable harm

[
24
]

Mr. N. G. is currently under confinement in a closed unit and according to
the evidence, his current state requires treatment. The lack of treatment to
stabilize and improve his current mental state of health is likely to cause him
serious harm because of his inappropriate, intimidating and harassing conduct
which has an impact on his psychosocial and daily functioning.

[
25
]

The treatment plan, once administered, should
have positive impact on his capacity to function properly and eventually provide
him with more latitude to retain his own expert and contest the Application,
should he decide to do so.

2.4.

Balance of inconveniences

[
26
]

For the same reasons, the evidence convinces the Court that the balance of inconveniences
favors the issuance of a safeguard order for an authorization of treatment.

[
27
]

A temporary and limited authorization for pharmacological
treatment of Mr. N. G.’s psychotic decompensation appears, in light of the
evidence and despite its potential side effects, preferable to an absence of
treatment which would maintain him in a state of delusion, paranoia and
distress.

WHEREFORE, THE COURT:

[
28
]

ISSUES
the
following safeguard order to be valid until December 16, 2019 at 5pm;

[
29
]

AUTHORIZES
Plaintiffs to provide the necessary documents
and information contained in Defendant’s medical record to the Court for the
purpose of the Application;

[
30
]

CONFIRMS
Defendant’s incapacity to
consent to the proposed treatment plan;

[
31
]

AUTHORIZES
Plaintiffs,
and any institution, physician or person designated by them, to administer the
following treatment plan to Defendant;

a)

Administration of an antipsychotic medication in oral form, such as
aripiprazole (Abilify) 10 mg daily, or long-acting injectable form, such as
aripiprazole (Abilify Maintena) 400 mg every three (3) to (4) weeks, or any
other equivalent medication, alone or in combination, at
the dose and frequency prescribed and adjusted by Defendant’s treating doctor,
in accordance with Defendant’s clinical evolution;

b)

Administration of any medications that Defendant may require
to manage the side effects of the antipsychotic medications, including without
limitation antiparkinsonian medication (Cogentin) 1 mg orally twice daily,
alone or in combination, at the dose and frequency prescribed
and adjusted by Defendant’s treating doctor, in accordance with
Defendant’s clinical evolution;

c)

Administration of basic care, minimally-invasive
investigations, tests and exams, such as vital signs monitoring and blood
tests, that may be required to allow Defendant’s treating team to monitor
Defendant’s condition and clinical evolution;

d)

Follow-up with an outpatient psychiatric team, such as a ‘’Suivi
intensif dans le milieu’’ (‘’SIM’’) team or the outpatient psychiatry clinic of
the Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital, or any other type of
follow-up, as deemed appropriate by Defendant’s treating team according to his
medical and psychosocial condition;

[
32
]

AUTHORIZES
Plaintiffs to pursue
Defendant’s hospitalization until a safe discharge plan is in place for
Defendant and his condition is stable enough to allow his
discharge, which shall be for the shortest period possible according to his
clinical and psychosocial condition;

[
33
]

ORDERS
that, if Defendant does
not comply with the treatment plan, or if Defendant’s clinical situation
deteriorates and that his treating team believes he requires hospitalization,
he be transported to the Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital or to
any other hospital setting by ambulance or a peace officer, upon request of any
member of Defendant’s treating team, and be hospitalized so that his medical
and psychiatric condition may be reassessed and treatment may be resumed within
the briefest delay, until his condition is stable enough to allow his
discharge, which shall be for the shortest period possible according to his
clinical and psychosocial condition;

[
34
]

ORDERS
any peace
officer to use the necessary means, including the necessary force, to assist
Plaintiffs or any institution or physician in the execution of the judgment, if
Defendant refuses to comply with the judgment;

[
35
]

THE WHOLE
, without legal costs.

SUZANNE COURCHESNE, S.C.J.

Me Andréane Baribeau
